analysis.one_liner: Speeds up the 2001 income-tax cuts, slashes dividend and capital-gains taxes, and sends $20 billion to states.
analysis.headline: Passed along party lines and signed into law on May 28, 2003: the House vote was 222-203, and the final Senate vote on the conference report was 51-50, with the Vice President's tie-breaking vote deciding it.
analysis.plain_summary: This law moved tax cuts originally scheduled to phase in over years into 2003: the child tax credit rose to $1,000 with advance checks mailed to families, marriage-penalty relief and the new lower income-tax rates took effect immediately, and the alternative minimum tax exemption rose. It cut the tax rate on dividends and long-term capital gains to 5 and 15 percent, quadrupled the small-business equipment-expensing allowance, offered 50 percent bonus depreciation on new equipment, and gave states $20 billion in temporary Medicaid and general aid. The individual and investment tax cuts carry expiration dates — the dividend and capital-gains provisions end after 2008, and the individual provisions inherit the expiration dates from the 2001 tax law.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children received $400 advance checks per child in 2003 [S7]. Married couples got immediate relief from the marriage penalty and higher-income workers got the accelerated cut to the 28, 33, and 35 percent rates [S7]. Stock owners — a group concentrated among higher-income households — got the largest new break: dividends taxed at 15 percent (5 percent for lower-income investors) and long-term capital gains at 15 percent, replacing rates as high as 38.6 and 20 percent [S7]. Businesses that buy equipment could immediately expense up to $100,000 (up from $25,000) and deduct half the cost of new equipment right away [S7]. States received $20 billion in one-time Medicaid and general-purpose aid during a recession [S7].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families, investors, and businesses buying equipment

how_it_helps.text: Sent $400-per-child advance payments to families who claimed the child tax credit, refunding the 2003 credit increase before October 1, 2003.
Cut the top individual income-tax rates (28, 31, 36, 39.6 percent) to 25, 28, 33, and 35 percent immediately instead of phasing in by 2006.

Cut the tax on corporate dividends and long-term capital gains to 15 percent (5 percent in the lowest brackets, 0 percent in 2008), down from rates up to 38.6 percent on dividends and 20 percent on gains.
Raised the small-business equipment expensing allowance from $25,000 to $100,000 through 2005 and included off-the-shelf computer software.
Provided $10 billion in increased Medicaid payments to states and $10 billion in general fiscal relief for essential government services through September 30, 2004.

Raised the alternative minimum tax exemptions to $58,000 (joint) and $40,250 (single) for 2003 and 2004, shielding middle- and upper-middle-income taxpayers from a parallel tax originally aimed at the very wealthy.

analysis.who_pays: The cuts are not paid for inside the bill: no revenue-raising offset accompanies roughly $350 billion of tax reductions, so the federal deficit and debt absorb the cost, a burden that falls on future taxpayers. Because the most valuable new break — the dividend and capital-gains rate cut — flows only to households that own taxable investments, and stock ownership is concentrated in higher-income households, the distribution of the benefits skews heavily toward the top. Low-income working families lost out specifically: the Senate version had extended the $1,000 child credit to millions of low-income working families who earned too little to receive the full increase, and the conference dropped that provision (widely reported).

drawbacks.text: The bill's tax cuts are not offset by spending cuts or tax increases anywhere in the law, so federal borrowing covers the cost; the total cost of the 2003 cuts is conventionally estimated at about $350 billion over a decade.
The dividend and capital-gains cut is worth most to households with large taxable investment portfolios; a family with no taxable stock gains receives nothing from the bill's signature Title III.

The conference committee dropped the Senate-passed provision that would have extended the $1,000 child credit to millions of low-income working families who earned more than the old threshold but too little to owe enough tax to get the full credit (widely reported).

The individual provisions expire after 2010 under the 2001 law's sunset and the investment provisions expire after 2008, so the relief families received was temporary and the tax code's long-term shape stayed uncertain.
The law lets corporations defer 25 percent of their September 2003 estimated tax payments until October 1, a two-week interest-free timing shift to corporate cash flow at the Treasury's expense.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Most households did receive a real, immediate tax cut — the $400-per-child checks, marriage-penalty relief, and lower rates were broad. But the bill's most distinctive and largest new break, the dividend and capital-gains rate cut, concentrates its value among households that own stocks, which are disproportionately wealthy, and the entire package is deficit-financed. The conference also stripped the one provision designed to reach the lowest-income working families. So the law is best read as a broad-but-temporary middle-income cut wrapped around a large, more durable tax cut for investors and equipment-buying businesses, with the bill for future deficits.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 222-203, passed the Senate 51-49, and after a conference committee trimmed some provisions, the final report cleared the House 231-200 and the Senate 51-50 with the Vice President breaking the tie; the President signed it on May 28, 2003.

narrative.text: The House Ways and Means Committee reported the bill on a 24-15 vote on May 6, 2003, and the House passed it 222-203 on May 9.
Senate Democrats' attempt to require the tax cuts not take effect until the federal budget was balanced failed 202-218 in the House, with all but one voting Republican against it.
The Senate passed its own version 51-49 on May 15, with three Democrats joining all but three Republicans.

The Senate version had included a provision extending the $1,000 child credit to low-income working families and had required corporations to pay only 48 percent of their September estimated taxes on time; the conference report dropped the child-credit expansion for low-income families (widely reported) and softened the corporate deferral to 25 percent delayed two weeks.

The conference report passed the House 231-200 and the Senate 51-50, with the Vice President's tie-breaking vote deciding it, and the President signed it into law as Public Law 108-27 on May 28, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income investors and equipment-buying businesses got the most valuable and least temporary parts of the law, while the conference committee's deletion of the low-income child-credit fix and the deficit financing left future taxpayers and low-wage working families with the smallest shares. State governments got real one-time relief that protected Medicaid and services.

for.name: George W. Bush

sides.party_line_note: The votes split almost entirely by party: House passage was 222-203 with 218 of 229 Republicans yes and only 4 of 205 Democrats yes; the final Senate vote was 51-50 with 48 of 51 Republicans yes, 2 of 48 Democrats yes, and the Vice President breaking the tie.

industries.note: Dividends and long-term capital gains were cut to 15 percent (5 percent at low incomes), a break that only flows to households with taxable investments — a group concentrated in the top income brackets. The cut was not offset anywhere in the bill, so the gain is financed by federal borrowing.

Corporations could defer 25 percent of their September 2003 estimated tax payment to October 1 at no interest cost, and buyers of new equipment got a 50 percent immediate depreciation deduction. The conference committee scaled the deferral back from the House version's 52 percent delayed a month.

50 percent bonus depreciation on new equipment placed in service through 2004 and the quadrupled expensing allowance were designed to spur equipment purchases, boosting demand for the manufacturers that sell it.

The Section 179 expensing limit rose from $25,000 to $100,000 through 2005 (with the phase-out threshold rising to $400,000) and was extended to off-the-shelf computer software, letting small firms deduct equipment and software costs immediately.

$20 billion in temporary aid — $10 billion in higher Medicaid payments and $10 billion for essential government services — helped states close recession-driven budget gaps without cutting Medicaid eligibility or public services; states that cut Medicaid eligibility forfeited the money.
